results.answer:
A measure family is a governed analytical family that carries one semantic identity and a declared family law. It is the named “what” of an analytical quantity (for example, Revenue) independent of any particular location where it is evaluated [S7].

A measure is that family at one anchor: Measure = MeasureFamily @ Anchor. So “Revenue@Month”, “Revenue@Store”, or “Revenue@{Store,Month}” are measures from the Revenue family at those anchors [S2][S3]. The family organizes these measures and governs their lawful relations. Measures in the same family may reduce or relate according to the family’s law (for example, an additive law), but being in one family does not mean every anchor is reachable from every other (week and month may be incomparable) [S3].

Architecturally, a measure family is the basic algebraic unit for local coherence and path compression; families are the nodes of the governed analytical lineage graph, which carries ancestry and identity across families [S6].

Version note: In Version 6, what Version 5 called a “measure” is now called a “measure family,” and the old term “member” is retired; what was a “member” is now simply a “measure” written as Family@Anchor [S5].

Citations: [S7], [S2], [S3], [S6], [S5]

results.answer:
An anchor is the governed way we fix “where” analysis lives in a universe. Formally, it is a complete, disjoint partition of the universe’s root points; each block of that partition is an anchor point. This is stronger than an arbitrary grouping label: for example, a store anchor partitions all root points by store, and a {store, day} anchor partitions them by each governed store–day block [S1].

Equivalently, an anchor is a typed coordinate schema assembled by choosing one level on each declared axis; its point space is the product of those chosen levels, and an anchor point is one typed location in that space (e.g., Patient 17 × Visit 4 × Assay A is one point, not just a database key) [S5].

Anchors are not just structure; they carry analytical location. A measure is a measure family at one anchor (Measure = MeasureFamily @ Anchor), and each measure has one current anchor that says where it lives analytically [S3][S8].

Anchors can be related by admitted coarsenings: there is a (unique) map from A to A′ when each chosen level on every axis coarsens along its declared hierarchy; because per‑axis hierarchies are trees, between two anchors there is at most one such map [S2].

results.answer:
AT names the output anchor — the grain at which the query’s results are produced. It says “return this measure per these levels,” e.g. AT {customer} yields one result per customer [S1]. Inside an expression, a reducer may also carry its own input anchor (the pin) with @ {...} to state the series it reduces; that is separate from AT. In the example FROM product_manifold SELECT mean(engagement_score @ {customer, week}) AT {customer}, the mean reduces weekly engagement within each customer (the input anchor), and the final numbers are returned per customer (the output anchor via AT) [S1].

The framework adjudicates the reducer’s input pin against the output grain set by AT: (1) the pin may not be coarser than the output (REFUSE), and (2) no redundant pin when two pin levels are functionally cross-comparable (CLARIFY with the admissible choices) [S8]. This is why mean requires its input anchor to be explicit while AT determines where that computed value lands [S1][S8].

results.answer:
The four moods are the governed outcomes the system uses to answer any request — every answer is returned as a pair: the result and its context, in one of serve, disclose, clarify, or refuse [S1]. In the shipped Frame‑QL/Columna wire, they are defined this way, with no fifth outcome [S2]:

- Serve: Lawful and clean. All preconditions are verified or corroborated; no material soundness finding applies. The answer is returned with a single OK annotation [S2].
- Disclose: Lawful and determinate, but one or more material soundness findings accompany the answer. The system still serves the result, and the findings ride with it. A first‑class subcase is route‑around: the planner dissolves a risk (for example, recomputing from detail instead of using a stale or contradicted pre‑aggregate) and discloses the routing as information rather than surfacing a risk that no longer exists [S2].
- Clarify: Not executable as asked because several lawful meanings remain. No result is returned; the system names exactly what is underdetermined and what would determine it (how the clarification is conducted is a surface choice) [S2].
- Refuse: The request is well‑formed but no lawful path exists to produce a result — for example the data is not there, a declared governance rule withholds it, or the governed law does not grant the operation. No result is returned; the reason and remedy are stated. In current shipped law this is called refuse (earlier “inform” in a prior edition); structurally prohibited reductions always refuse and cannot be legalized by disclosing risk [S2][S7].

Additional notes:
- The moods sort by lawfulness, not by confidence: serve (lawful, no material condition), disclose (lawful, condition travels), clarify (several lawful meanings remain), refuse (no lawful path) [S2].
- A cross_universe category error is not a mood; it rides the separate query‑error channel [S2][S7].
- As a structural reading: refuse and clarify are the voice of structure, disclose is bookkeeping made explicit, and serve is the mood of no unresolved freedom [S6].
- “Every answer comes back in one of four moods” is part of the surrounding law; paired with “every answer is a pair — the result and its context — so whoever is asking always knows what they are standing on” [S1].

results.answer:
A basis is the account of point‑provenance for a universe — the rule that says which points exist in that population of facts. It is declared on a universe and governs the grid you evaluate on; columns bind to that named universe in their column‑spec [S2][S1].

The four shipped basis forms and what “points exist because …” means:
- registry(<entity_list>): an enumerated roster says so (a membership list) [S1].
- spine(<dimension>, …): a generator constructs the expected series (e.g., calendar days, hours) [S1].
- product(<universe>, …): the cross of factors (e.g., active_stores × calendar_day) [S1].
- events(<root>[, project = <anchor>]): points exist where something happened (e.g., observed transactions; customer‑days with purchases) [S1].

Two important clarifications:
- What the basis decides: whether a point is on the grid at all. For events, “nothing happened” means there is no point; for spine/product, the full grid is expected and a missing row is a gap the system can disclose as incomplete_data [S5].
- What the basis does not decide: what an absent value at an existing point denotes. That meaning (zero, unknown, or outside the population) is the measure’s fill rule Φ, not the basis [S4].

Declaration mechanics and reuse:
- UNIVERSE <name> BASIS <basis> declares the named point set once; columns reference it by name via ON, which is what enables verifiable co‑universality [S2][S1].
- A column rooted at its own grain lands on that root’s events projection by derivation; re‑declaring that projection is rejected as noise. The events(...) form exists so several columns can reuse the same named projection explicitly [S2].
